LESSON OBJECTIVE
Calculate trapezoid area and solve for a missing base or perpendicular height.
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW
A trapezoid has two parallel bases. Its area equals their average length multiplied by the perpendicular height.
KEY DEFINITIONS
The bases b₁ and b₂ are parallel. Height h is perpendicular to them, not a sloping leg. Midsegment=(b₁+b₂)/2.
CORE RULE
A=(b₁+b₂)h/2. For height use h=2A/(b₁+b₂). For missing base use b₂=2A/h−b₁.
HOW IT WORKS
Mark parallel bases and perpendicular height; convert units; add bases; multiply by height; divide by two; report square units.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1
Bases 6 cm and 10 cm, height 4 cm: A=(6+10)×4/2=32 cm². Check the exact-scale diagram.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2
Bases 8 m and 12 m, height 5 m: average base 10 m, so A=10×5=50 m².
WORKED EXAMPLE 3
Area 63 cm², bases 7 and 14 cm: h=2×63/(7+14)=6 cm. Check: 21×6/2=63.
WORKED EXAMPLE 4
Area 72 m², height 8 m, one base 6 m: base sum=2×72/8=18 m, so other base=12 m.
WORKED EXAMPLE 5
Trapezoid bases 10 and 18 m, height 7 m: area=98 m². Subtract a triangular bed of area 6 m² to leave 92 m².
VERIFIED GEOMETRY DIAGRAM
The diagram uses a consistent scale: upper base 6, lower base 10, perpendicular height 4. Exact area is 32 square units.
MIDSEGMENT SHORTCUT
Midsegment is average base. With midsegment 11 cm and height 7 cm, area=77 cm².
ALGEBRAIC BASES
Bases x+2 and x+8, height 6, area 90: 90=(2x+10)×3, so x=10. Both base lengths must be positive.
SIMILARITY
If every length is scaled by k, area is scaled by k². Area 96 scaled by 1.5 becomes 216.
COMMON MISTAKES
Never use a sloping leg as the height; remember to divide by two and convert units; area uses squared units.
EXAM STRATEGY AND QUICK CHECK
Draw the perpendicular height first. Bases 4 and 8, height 5 give area 30. Area 84, bases 8 and 16 give height 7.
LESSON RECAP AND NEXT STEP
